content.text: How can understanding another person’s perspective strengthen relationships and community?
By noticing and sharing small moments, people build empathy, voice, and community.
In Lesson 27, students will practice using pacing to write an original story about a character from the anchor text.
Knowledge of narrative writing, with a focus on pacing, is key to the performance task.
Look Both Ways
by Jason Reynolds
Unit 1 Lesson 30 Student Edition
Timeline graphic organizer
Discuss how stories can build empathy and community using both the anchor text (fiction) and an excerpt from a nonfictional article about middle school.
Argue how specific craft choices (especially pacing) build empathy by stating a clear claim, citing text evidence from
Look Both Ways
, and using discussion stems to build on or challenge peers’ ideas.
Students will discuss how stories can build empathy and community using both the anchor text (fiction) and an excerpt from a nonfictional article about middle school.
Students will argue how specific craft choices (especially pacing) build empathy by stating a clear claim, citing text evidence from
Look Both Ways
, and using discussion stems to build on or challenge peers’ ideas.
Turn and Talk

Quick Write
Turn and Talk
Directions:

Discuss your response to the prompts at the end of the previous lesson with a partner. How do you think adults view kids your age? Has there been a time recently when you felt that you were unfairly judged because of your age? What would you like adults to know about middle schoolers?
How does sharing our stories help build community and empathy?
We all want to be understood, and when we understand each other, we can build community and empathy. Stories can be a great way to help us understand others and even ourselves.
Directions:
Choose a vignette from
Look Both Ways
and think about how it helped you better understand a character, another person, or yourself. As you discuss, explain how the author’s choices helped create that understanding.

When you share, name the vignette, identify a specific craft choice (such as pacing, structure, or dialogue), and explain how that choice helps the reader better understand the character or situation.
Part A: Building Empathy and Understanding: “Middle School is More Than You Think”
Directions:
Follow along as the article is read aloud, and think about its main ideas about middle school. As you listen, notice ideas or details that connect to empathy, understanding, and community.

Work with a partner to summarize the article and connect its ideas to what you discussed during the Launch. Be ready to explain the article’s central idea and what it suggests people should understand about middle schoolers.
How would you summarize this article? Does this article address any of the things you wish people would understand about being in middle school? Discuss with your partner for two minutes.
How does this article help support the essential question “How does sharing our stories help build community and empathy?” Discuss with your partner for two minutes.
Pulse Check
Which statement provides the best summary of the article “Middle School is More Than You Think”?
Middle school can be fun, but only hard, serious work can make it effective.
Middle school can be a challenging time, but with understanding, supportive teaching, and strong relationships, students can grow and succeed.
Middle school can be boring, and student misbehavior can make it chaotic.
Part B: Pacing and Empathy in
Look Both Ways
Pacing Directions:

Today, you will look closely at how pacing works in “What Middle Schoolers Actually Need.” As you track events on the timeline, think about how the author reveals information over time and how that changes the way readers understand the characters.
Authors have to carefully choose how to combine description, action, and dialogue so that the reader stays interested in the characters.
Remember that
pacing
is how quickly or slowly an author introduces different characters, ideas, or events as the story goes on.
The events of the story take place in just about an hour, from the end-of-school bell until a few minutes after 4 p.m. But pacing is about how the events of that hour are fed to the reader.
Directions:
Label the timeline with the events as they happen in the story. What are some of the major events of this story, and where do they fit along the timeline?

Then, label the events on the timeline as either description, dialogue, or action. As you do this, think about how each type of information is revealed and how it shapes your understanding of the characters over time.
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of pacing in “The Low Cuts Strike Again” using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to discuss a story’s pacing?

Rate your confidence level on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 being the least confident and 5 being the most confident. Then write a sentence or two describing what parts of today’s discussion were the easiest and most difficult for you to understand and why.
Fishbowl Conversation
How does the pacing in this story help build empathy?
Directions:

Half of you will begin in the inner circle and discuss how pacing in this story helps build empathy, while the other half will observe, listen closely, and take notes. Then you will switch roles. Use details from the timeline and the story to support your ideas and respond to what others say.
Sample prompt
What do we know about the Low Cuts at the very beginning, a few pages in, and at the end? How does this information change how we view them? You have five minutes to discuss.
How does the author create expectations and tension about the characters? How does the title play a part in that?
How does the author use those expectations later in the story to help build empathy?
Checklist
Look to make sure you:
Draw on prior reading to cite specific textual evidence to support your ideas.
Ask and answer specific questions related to the prompt to build on the answers of your peers and contribute meaningfully to the discussion.
Show understanding of key ideas by paraphrasing the text and/or the ideas of your peers.
Quick Write
What are possible effects of a story’s pacing?
Turn and Talk
Instruct students to take out their homework from the previous lesson.

Lesson 25 Homework: Students were instructed to answer the following prompts in their Journal: How do you think adults view kids your age? Has there been a time recently when you felt that you were unfairly judged because of your age? What would you like adults to know about middle schoolers?
Instruct students to share their response from the previous lesson’s homework with a partner. Even if students have not completed the homework, they can still discuss the prompts.
Say these Directions:

Discuss your response to the prompts at the end of the previous lesson with a partner. How do you think adults view kids your age? Has there been a time recently when you felt that you were unfairly judged because of your age? What would you like adults to know about middle schoolers?
People should understand how creative, funny, and kind middle schoolers can be.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:

Today, we are going to explore how stories—both fictional and nonfiction—can challenge assumptions about middle schoolers and help people build understanding, empathy, and community. We will also examine how authors make specific craft choices to shape those stories effectively.
Students will discuss and share their written responses to the homework prompt.
Display Essential Question 2, and note its connection to the questions students just discussed during the Launch.
How does sharing our stories help build community and empathy?
Relate the idea of building community and empathy to understanding middle school students better, both of which can be built through telling effective stories.
Say:
We all want to be understood, and when we understand each other, we can build community and empathy. Stories can be a great way to help us understand others and even ourselves.
Connect this idea to some of the vignettes in
Look Both Ways
, and prompt a discussion in which students share vignettes that helped them better understand a character, a classmate, or themselves.
Say these Directions:
Choose a vignette from
Look Both Ways
and think about how it helped you better understand a character, another person, or yourself. As you discuss, explain how the author’s choices helped create that understanding.
Begin by modeling a response.
Say:

The vignette “How to Look (Both) Both Ways” helped me understand Fatima, my friends, and myself. Seeing Fatima’s list of what changed and what stayed the same and then seeing how the list changed based on her experiences, really helped me understand how nervous she was about walking home alone and how much meeting Benni changed her point of view. It also helped me understand how some of my friends can get so worried about small changes in our routines. It also helped me realize how many lists of my own I keep, just in my head, not on paper. I think change and new experiences can be hard for everyone, and it’s good to understand that everybody is dealing with them all the time.
Prompt students to share and discuss their own examples.
Say:

When you share, name the vignette, identify a specific craft choice (such as pacing, structure, or dialogue), and explain how that choice helps the reader better understand the character or situation.

The vignette “Skitter Hitter” helped me understand Marcus as a character, and some of my classmates at school. I got so mad when Marcus was mean to Stevie and Pia. From Pia’s point of view, I learned about how hard Marcus’s homelife is and how embarrassed he got the first time they played together. This helped me understand how Marcus and some of my classmates might act mean because they’re hurt or embarrassed. Maybe we’d all be nicer to each other if we understood those things better.
Support students in turning “A story helped me understand . . .” into an argument about craft by stating a claim about a vignette’s craft choice and explaining how it builds empathy.
Require each student to share: vignette + craft choice + empathy effect (not just a summary).
Prompt students to name the craft choice precisely (pacing, structure, dialogue, symbolism, word choice) and connect it to a reader reaction.
After 2–3 shares, synthesize aloud with a class “craft claim” sentence that students can reuse.
Press for empathy link: “So how does that make a reader understand the character differently?”
“In the vignette ‘___,’ the author uses ___ (craft choice) to ___, which builds empathy because ___.”
“One detail that supports my idea is ___.”
“This made me understand ___ (character) as ___ because ___.”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become more independent.
Emerging:
"When the author slows down ___, it shows ___." / "This part made me feel ___."
Expanding:
"The pacing here shows ___ because ___." / "According to the text, ___ builds empathy by ___."
Bridging:
"By pacing this moment as ___, the author emphasizes ___." / "Taken together, these craft choices ___."
Validate multiple interpretations: students can disagree about the empathy effect as long as they cite a specific craft move and a supporting detail.
Revoice “It’s sad” → “The pacing/word choice creates sadness because ___.”
Upgrade “It shows” → “It reveals/highlights/suggests ___.”
If student gives plot only → Prompt: “Name the craft move (pacing/structure/dialogue) and the effect on the reader.”
If student names craft but no evidence → Prompt: “Add one specific moment (what happens/what’s revealed/what’s repeated).”
Students name a craft choice accurately.
Students link craft → reader understanding/empathy.
Students cite at least one specific text detail (moment, reveal, repetition, or structural move).

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Names one pacing moment and a reaction; points to evidence.
Expanding:
Explains how pacing creates empathy; cites specific moments with brief reasoning.
Bridging:
Argues how pacing (and other craft moves) build empathy; cites precise moments and links craft → effect.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:

Today, we’re going to compare how a fictional text and a nonfiction article both help readers understand middle school experiences and build empathy, and we’ll look closely at the author choices that make that understanding possible.
Students will discuss which vignettes from
Look Both Ways
helped them understand a character, a classmate, or themselves better.
Part A: Building Empathy and Understanding: “Middle School is More Than You Think” (RI.6.2, SL.6.1.c) (10 minutes)
Have students take out their copies of “Middle School is More Than You Think.” Have students follow along as you read the article aloud.
Say these Directions:
Follow along as the article is read aloud, and think about its main ideas about middle school. As you listen, notice ideas or details that connect to empathy, understanding, and community.
Display the excerpt and read the introduction and first section aloud, pausing briefly to clarify key ideas. Students will then work in pairs to discuss the text.
Say:

Work with a partner to summarize the article and connect its ideas to what you discussed during the Launch. Be ready to explain the article’s central idea and what it suggests people should understand about middle schoolers.
Display and say the following prompt.
Ask:
How would you summarize this article? Does this article address any of the things you wish people would understand about being in middle school? Discuss with your partner for two minutes.

The article says that most people think of middle school as just being a really tough time, but it can also be a great opportunity for learning and growing. It also says that there are a lot of ways that schools and teachers are trying to change how they teach and talk to middle schoolers to help them feel included and supported. The central idea is that middle schoolers are often misunderstood, but with the right support and understanding, they can succeed and feel more connected. It says some of the things I wish people would understand about middle school, like how we need more creative teaching, but I wish it talked about some of the harder parts, like feeling left out.
Return to Essential Question 2, and prompt students to discuss it further in relation to the article.
Display and say the following prompt.
Ask:
How does this article help support the essential question “How does sharing our stories help build community and empathy?” Discuss with your partner for two minutes.

The article explains that middle schoolers are often misunderstood, but when people learn more about what they are going through—like changes in their brains, emotions, and social lives—they can better understand their behavior. This helps build empathy because it shows that students aren’t just being difficult; they are growing and learning. When people understand these experiences, they are more likely to be patient and supportive, which helps build a stronger community.
Help students use article evidence to build a claim about empathy/community by quoting or paraphrasing a specific line and explaining how it supports Essential Question 2.
Encourage students to connect article ideas to school/community experiences without requiring personal disclosure (“In schools, people might . . .”).
Require students to anchor claims in one specific article detail (a quote, paraphrase, or named speaker).
Push students to distinguish: claim (what the article argues) vs. evidence (what line shows it) vs. explanation (how it supports Essential Question 2).
Model one “Because ___, therefore ___” chain using a student-friendly paraphrase.
Add precision connectors: “as a result,” “therefore,” “this matters because . . .”
“The article’s central idea is ___.”
“One detail that supports this is ___, which shows ___.”
“This connects to EQ2 because ___, so ___.”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“The article says ___.” / “This connects to empathy because ___.”
Expanding:
“The author argues/suggests ___, which implies ___.”
Bridging:
“The author argues ___ (quote/paraphrase), which implies ___; in schools, this might look like ___, connecting to the Essential Question because ___.”
Revoice “It says teachers should . . .” → “The author argues/suggests ___, which implies ___.”
Upgrade “helps community” → “builds empathy by ___” / “reduces judgment by ___.”
If response is opinion only → Prompt: “Add one article detail (a name, a quote, or a paraphrase).”
If evidence is too vague (“it said ...”) → Prompt: “Name the speaker/author + restate 6–10 key words.”
Students state a claim about the article’s message.
Students include one concrete article detail.
Students explain how the detail supports empathy/community (not just summary).
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Quotes or paraphrases one line from the article using a frame.
Expanding:
Pairs an article line with a claim about empathy/community; explains how it supports the Essential Question.
Bridging:
Builds a claim using article evidence + community connection + explanation; uses precise verbs (argues, suggests, implies).
Teacher Tip

This conversation could veer into topics that may be difficult for students to discuss. Do your best to strike a balance between making the classroom a safe place to have difficult conversations and letting students know that they are never under any pressure to share any personal experiences that they would rather not share.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Building Empathy and Understanding

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Relating the text to the essential question
Try rephrasing the essential question to bring the language closer to some of the quotes in the article. Ex. “How does hearing real stories help you learn different ideas?”
Struggling with: Summarizing the central idea
Prompt: What is the article mostly about? What is one important idea the author wants readers to understand about middle school?
Ready for extension: Relating the text to the essential question
Ask:

After reading this article, what is one thing you think we could do differently at this school to build more community and empathy? I think we could have more physical activities in class, because it would help the people who just can’t sit still. Everyone would then feel included and part of the school community.
Pulse Check (RI.6.2)
Which statement provides the best summary of the article “Middle School is More Than You Think”?
Middle school can be fun, but only hard, serious work can make it effective.
Incorrect: The article focuses on how people can better understand and support middle schoolers, not just increase rigor.
Middle school can be a challenging time, but with understanding, supportive teaching, and strong relationships, students can grow and succeed.
Correct: This statement captures the article’s central idea that middle school is complex but can be positive when students are supported and understood.
Middle school can be boring, and student misbehavior can make it chaotic.
Incorrect: The article emphasizes growth, understanding, and support rather than focusing mainly on negative behavior.
Part B: Pacing and Empathy in
Look Both Ways
(RL.6.3, SL.6.1.c) (20 minutes)
Display the
Timeline graphic organize
r, and hand out copies to students.
Teach: Pacing
Say these Directions:

Today, you will look closely at how pacing works in “What Middle Schoolers Actually Need.” As you track events on the timeline, think about how the author reveals information over time and how that changes the way readers understand the characters.
Remind students of the idea and importance of pacing in a story.
Say:
If you ever start to feel bored when you are reading a story, it might be because the pace is too slow!
Say:
Authors have to carefully choose how to combine description, action, and dialogue so that the reader stays interested in the characters.
Remember that
pacing
is how quickly or slowly an author introduces different characters, ideas, or events as the story goes on.
The events of the story take place in just about an hour, from the end-of-school bell until a few minutes after 4 p.m. But pacing is about how the events of that hour are fed to the reader.
Briefly remind students of the basic plot of “The Low Cuts Strike Again” from
Look Both Ways
. Lead a class discussion on how the plot unfolds over the course of the story, and record students’ plot points on the timeline.
Say these Directions:
Label the timeline with the events as they happen in the story. What are some of the major events of this story, and where do they fit along the timeline?
Say:
Looking at our timeline, we can see how we gradually learn more and more about the Low Cuts.
Say these Directions:

Now, label the events on the timeline as either description, dialogue, or action. As you do this, think about how each type of information is revealed and how it shapes your understanding of the characters over time.
Provide students with a confidence continuum (i.e., 1–5). As needed, model how to demonstrate a level of confidence using the continuum.
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of pacing in “The Low Cuts Strike Again” using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to discuss a story’s pacing?

Rate your confidence level on a scale of 1 to 5, with 1 being the least confident and 5 being the most confident. Then write a sentence or two describing what parts of today’s discussion were the easiest and most difficult for you to understand and why.
Fishbowl Conversation
Have students work in two large groups for
a Fishbowl Conversatio
n based on the following prompt:
How does the pacing in this story help build empathy?
Remind students of how the
Fishbowl Conversation
s routine works, and model playing both parts.
Say these Directions:

Half of you will begin in the inner circle and discuss how pacing in this story helps build empathy, while the other half will observe, listen closely, and take notes. Then you will switch roles. Use details from the timeline and the story to support your ideas and respond to what others say.
Say:

Someone in the inner circle might say, “It really changes how you look at the Low Cuts when the narrator mentions all their parents are cancer survivors.” Someone else might agree and say, “I was kind of judging them before that, and then I felt bad.” Meanwhile, people in the outer circle will listen and take notes.

Arrange the two groups of students into an inner and outer circle, and give the inner circle five minutes to discuss the prompt while the outer circle observes. Prompt students in the inner circle as necessary to keep the discussion going.
Display sample prompt.
Ask:
What do we know about the Low Cuts at the very beginning, a few pages in, and at the end? How does this information change how we view them? You have five minutes to discuss.

At the beginning, we learn that they steal from everybody. Then we learn that they’re poor, their parents are cancer survivors, and they don’t steal for fun. Then we learn that they were stealing today so they can buy Bit’s mom ice cream. That changes how we view them. We move from thinking they’re bad to thinking maybe they have a good reason to be bad to seeing they’re not bad at all and are just helping their families.
After five minutes, have the two groups switch, and give the new inner circle another five minutes to discuss the prompt.
If time allows, lead a whole-class discussion about how the author uses expectations to tell the story and build empathy for the characters.
Ask:
How does the author create expectations and tension about the characters? How does the title play a part in that?

“Strike again” sounds like someone committed a crime or an attack and then did it again, so it sets up your expectation that the characters are bad criminals. Tension is created because the author starts the story by describing the Low Cuts as bad and letting the reader think that until their actions and conversations in the last few paragraphs.
Ask:
How does the author use those expectations later in the story to help build empathy?

First, the story creates tension and reinforces bad expectations when it introduces the Low Cuts by describing them as thieves. But the rest of the story gives more and more information that shows you that those expectations are wrong. This gives the reader more empathy for the Low Cuts and adjusts their expectations once they learn the whole story.
Support students in arguing that pacing builds empathy by using timeline language (beginning/middle/end), evidence-based reasoning, and discussion moves during the Fishbowl Conversation.
Require pacing language in each turn: “At the beginning . . . ,” “Later . . . ,” “By the end . . .”
During outer-circle note-taking, require students to record speaker claim + evidence moment + effect so they can respond with specificity.
Prompt contrast: “At first, readers assume ___; later, the text reveals ___; therefore, readers feel ___.”
“At the beginning, the story frames ___, so readers expect ___.”
“Later, we learn ___, which changes our view because ___.”
“By the end, the reveal about ___ builds empathy by ___.”
Discussion moves: “I want to build on ___ because ___.” “I challenge that because ___.” “Can you clarify what moment shows that?”
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“At the beginning, ___.” / “By the end, ___, which builds empathy because ___.”
Expanding:
“At the beginning, ___; later, ___; by the end, ___, which builds empathy because the pacing ___.”
Bridging:
“The pacing builds empathy by ___: at the beginning, ___; later, ___; by the end, ___; this sequence shapes how readers understand ___ because ___.”
Normalize revision of thinking: highlight that changing your mind after a reveal is evidence that pacing is working.
Give students a 3-step speaking routine for Fishbowl Conversation turns: claim → evidence (timeline moment) → empathy effect.
Revoice “we learn more later” → “The author delays key information, which shifts the reader’s judgment because ___.”
Upgrade “makes me feel bad” → “builds empathy by challenging expectations / revealing context.”
If student can’t connect pacing to empathy → Prompt: “What did you think at first, and what did you think after the reveal? Name the turning point.”
If student gives effect without evidence → Prompt: “Point to where on the timeline the shift happens (beginning/middle/end) and what new info appears.”
Students use pacing language (beginning/later/by the end).
Students cite a specific reveal/shift moment from “The Low Cuts Strike Again.”
Students explain empathy as a change in judgment/understanding, not just a feeling word.
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Uses one timeline phrase (At the beginning/Later/By the end); names one pacing moment.
Expanding:
Uses claim → evidence (timeline moment) → empathy effect in a single Fishbowl turn.
Bridging:
Sustains pacing-as-craft argument across turns; uses discussion moves and connects pacing to empathy effect with precise evidence.

attrs.label: Additional Student Support: Pacing and Empathy

content.text: Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Understanding pacing

Ask questions about when readers learn different pieces of information about the characters and why the author might have made those decisions. Ex. “How long does it take before we start learning more about why the Low Cuts steal? Why do you think the author wanted to wait that long? Did you change your mind about them as you read?”
Ready for extension: Pacing and empathy
Ask:

Can you sum up in one sentence what the author is trying to do with the pacing of this story? The author is trying to convey the message that sometimes you don’t know why people do what they do until you learn more about them, no matter how long that may take.
Checklist
Look to make sure you:
Draw on prior reading to cite specific textual evidence to support your ideas.
Ask and answer specific questions related to the prompt to build on the answers of your peers and contribute meaningfully to the discussion.
Show understanding of key ideas by paraphrasing the text and/or the ideas of your peers.
Part A: Building Empathy and Understanding (RI.6.2, SL.6.1.c)
Students will read and discuss the article excerpt and use it to share their own thoughts about what they would like others to understand about them.
Part B: Pacing and Empathy in Look Both Ways (RL.6.3, SL.6.1.c)
Students will discuss pacing in “The Low Cuts Strike Again,” focusing on how it can help create empathy by creating and subverting expectations about characters.
Quick Write
Instruct students to reflect on today’s discussion by writing a brief response to the following prompt.
Ask:
What are the possible effects of a story’s pacing?
Optional Sentence Starter:
“The pacing of a story can create a feeling of ____ in the reader by ____.”

The pacing of a story can create a feeling of tension in the reader. Authors can achieve this by playing with readers’ expectations, gradually giving information that challenges those expectations, and then moving the pace more quickly as the story goes on. This makes readers pay more attention to the ideas and characters because they want to know what happens next!
Students will write a brief reflection about how authors can use pacing and play with reader expectations to create tension in stories.
Inform students that in the next lesson, they will write an original narrative about an ordinary day or event in the life of a character from
Look Both Ways.
Instruct students to brainstorm and take notes in their
Journal
on the following prompts:
Choose the character from
Look Both Ways
you want to write about.
Invent a situation for your character that is not from the book.
Brainstorm ideas about how you want to use pacing to reveal the new event.

By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering detailed questions, with minimal prompting and support.
Demonstrate active listening in oral presentation activities by asking and answering basic questions, with prompting and substantial support.

content.text: How does sharing stories help people understand one another?
